analysis.one_liner: Set national data-breach notification and credit-freeze rules while overriding stronger state laws.
analysis.headline: Two House committees approved it by votes of 48-17 and 42-0, but the bill sat on the House calendar for seven months and never got a floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created one national standard requiring companies that handle consumer financial data to safeguard it, investigate suspected breaches, and notify affected consumers, along with free credit monitoring after a breach and free credit freezes for identity theft victims. But it also would have preempted stronger state breach-notification and credit-freeze laws, let companies skip notice when data was encrypted or fraud-detection software might catch misuse, limited freezes to identity theft victims only, and exempted credit monitoring services from the Credit Repair Organizations Act. Both House committees approved it, but it never received a floor vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers whose financial data is breached would get an investigation, notice, at least six months of free credit or identity monitoring paid for by the breached company, and a public FTC list of recent breaches [S3] [S5]. Identity theft victims could place a security freeze on their credit reports at no charge, with no fee to lift it [S3] [S5]. Anyone whose personal information an information broker holds would gain rights to review and correct it, and companies holding electronic personal data would face FTC security rules and a ban on pretexting [S4] [S5].

how_it_helps.text: Every company defined as a 'consumer reporter' — credit bureaus, banks, and others assembling or evaluating consumer financial data — would have to keep reasonable security procedures, immediately investigate suspected breaches, notify the Secret Service, regulators, and affected consumers, and repair its systems after a breach [S5].

Consumers who receive a breach notice could request at least six months of free nationwide credit monitoring or identity monitoring at the company's expense, and companies could not charge consumers for the cost of notices or monitoring [S3] [S5].

Identity theft victims could place a security freeze on their credit report free of charge — the credit bureau could not release the report without the victim's authorization — and could not charge a fee for placing, lifting, or removing it [S3] [S5].

The FTC would have to publish a public list of breaches that triggered consumer notices in the past 12 months, and the Energy and Commerce title would require the FTC to write information-security regulations for anyone holding electronic personal data, give individuals access to and correction of information-broker files, ban pretexting, and let state attorneys general sue violators [S3] [S4].

Treasury, the Federal Reserve, and the FTC would jointly write uniform data-security standards and model breach-notice forms, replacing a patchwork of agency guidance under the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act [S2] [S3] [S5].

analysis.who_pays: Companies that hold consumer financial data — banks, credit bureaus, lenders, data brokers, and any business holding electronic personal information — would bear the costs of breach investigations, consumer notices, six months of free monitoring, freeze administration, and new FTC security and audit requirements [S3] [S4] [S5]. The FTC, Treasury, the Federal Reserve, and other banking regulators would bear the cost of joint rulemaking, enforcement, audits, and mandated studies and a national summit [S3] [S4] [S5].
analysis.who_pays_short: Banks, credit bureaus, and data brokers

drawbacks.text: The bill would have overridden stronger state laws: it preempted state rules on data security, breach notice, and credit freezes, replacing laws that let any consumer freeze their credit with a federal rule allowing freezes only for identity theft victims who apply in writing by certified mail with a police identity-theft report [S5].

Companies could avoid notifying consumers if the stolen data was encrypted or otherwise unusable, or if their fraud-detection software was likely to catch fraudulent transactions — and a company that offered free monitoring would be shielded from liability for identity theft that followed the breach [S5].

It exempted credit monitoring services from the Credit Repair Organizations Act, weakening oversight of a business that profits directly from consumers' fear of breaches, so long as the service carries prescribed disclosures and cancellation rights [S3] [S5].

Enforcement would rest with the functional regulators that already oversee each financial company — banking regulators, the SEC, the FTC — through administrative proceedings, with the disclosure that violations be treated as regulatory matters rather than adding a route for consumers to sue [S5].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered real, concrete help — free monitoring after breaches, free freezes for victims, public breach lists, and new security duties for data brokers — and consumers in states with no or weak laws would have gained a national floor. But its design consistently favored the companies holding the data: the notice trigger was easier to avoid than most state laws, encryption and fraud-detection safe harbors let companies stay silent, the freeze right was narrower than what roughly two dozen states had already enacted, liability shields and the Credit Repair Organizations Act exemption protected revenue streams, and preemption would have locked in that weaker standard nationwide. An honest supporter would have to concede that consumers in stronger states — California above all — would have traded real rights for this federal floor.

outcome.mechanism: After clearing two House committees, the bill was placed on the House calendar on June 2, 2006 and was never brought up for a vote before the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Rep. Steven LaTourette introduced the bill on October 6, 2005, and it was referred to the House Financial Services Committee, which held a hearing in November 2005 [S2] [S7].
On March 16, 2006, the Financial Services Committee approved an amended version by a vote of 48-17, and it was reported on May 4, 2006 as House Report 109-454, Part I [S3] [S7].

The bill was sent sequentially to the Energy and Commerce Committee, which approved it 42-0 on May 24, 2006 and reported it on June 2, 2006 as Part II — a second title, the Data Accountability and Trust Act, covering information brokers, FTC security regulations, and state attorney general enforcement [S4] [S7].

That same day the bill was placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 269 — the list of bills awaiting House floor action — but no floor debate or vote ever occurred, and the bill died when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007 [S5] [S7].
No Senate companion ever advanced, so the bill never came close to becoming law [S1] [S7].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumers in states with stronger breach-notification and credit-freeze laws came out ahead, because those laws stayed in force instead of being replaced by the bill's weaker federal standard. Data-handling companies also avoided the bill's new compliance costs, while the broader winner was the status quo in which no national breach law was enacted.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Consumers protected by stronger state laws

sides.party_line_note: A Republican sponsor carried the bill with 24 cosponsors including 7 Democrats, the Energy and Commerce Committee reported it unanimously 42-0, and Financial Services approved it 48-17.

industries.note: The bill's biggest structural win for the bureaus was preemption: state laws letting any consumer freeze their credit — which cut into the sale of credit reports — would have been replaced by a freeze available only to identity theft victims. The Credit Repair Organizations Act exemption also freed the bureaus' credit monitoring products from credit-repair oversight, while the costs on them (six months of free monitoring after breaches, free victim freezes) were comparatively small.

Banks gained a single national standard with encryption safe harbors, an escape hatch from consumer notice when fraud-detection software might catch misuse, a liability shield for offering free monitoring, and preemption of stricter state rules — offset by duties to investigate breaches, notify consumers, and provide free monitoring. Their interest in easier-to-avoid notification ran against the consumers the notices protect.

Mandatory free monitoring after a breach gave these companies six months of direct contact with worried consumers, a well-known sales funnel into paid subscriptions, and the bill simultaneously exempted their products from the Credit Repair Organizations Act. Their revenue depends on breach fear, which cuts against measures like universal free credit freezes.

The Energy and Commerce title imposed real duties on brokers — security policies submitted to the FTC, audits after breaches, accuracy verification, individual access and correction rights, and a pretexting ban — but the same title preempted state information-security laws, trading new federal oversight for freedom from stricter state rules.

industries.industry: Companies holding electronic personal data (retailers, telecoms, and others)
industries.note: Beyond financial firms, the bill preempted state information-security laws for any company holding personal data, replacing whatever individual states had enacted with a single federal standard — the industry's central ask after the 2005 ChoicePoint-era breaches.
